title: Unique Neonatal Cardiovascular Problems

paragraphs.text: 77 Unique Neonatal Cardiovascular Problems
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The development of morphologically right-sided structures on one side of the body and morphologically left-sided structures on the other side is termed lateralization or situs. The normal disposition of organs in which right-sided structures are on the right side of the body, and vice versa, is known as situs solitus.1,2 The term viscero-atrial situs is often used to refer to the situs of the viscera, or noncardiac organs, and atria when their situs are in agreement. In normal atrial arrangement, or atrial situs solitus, the left atrium is on the left side and right atrium is on the right side. In atrial situs inversus, the left atrium is on the right side and the right atrium is on the left side. The relationship between the pulmonary artery and the bronchus is asymmetric. The right lung anatomically has an eparterial bronchus (i.e., one that branches superior to the first lobar division of the pulmonary artery), in contrast to the left-sided lung, which has a hyparterial bronchus (i.e., one that branches inferior to the first lobar division of the respective pulmonary artery) (Fig. 77.1).3
paragraphs.heading: Bodily Arrangement and Situs

paragraphs.text: Visceral situs solitus occurs when the abdominal organs are lateralized normally with the spleen and stomach on the left side and liver on the right side. Situs solitus implies normal viscero-atrial concordance, but there need not be atrioventricular or ventriculo-arterial concordance. A discordance at any level could cause clinical problems. A failure in the normal left-right asymmetry comes under a spectrum of laterality disturbances and is known as heterotaxia.4 Physical examination assisted by imaging studies such as ultrasound scan of the abdomen, computed tomography (CT) scan, or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) helps determine the lateralization of internal organs.
paragraphs.heading: Bodily Arrangement and Situs

paragraphs.text: Dextrocardia is present when the base to apex axis of the heart is directed to the right side of the chest.5 Another possible location for the heart is mesocardia, where the
paragraphs.heading: Bodily Arrangement and Situs

paragraphs.text: apex is in the midline. Situs solitus is the normal location of the atria and abdominal organs, as described previously. Situs inversus is present when the right atrium is on the left, the left atrium is on the right, and the liver and stomach are similarly reversed. Dextrocardia with situs inversus is referred to as the complete mirror image; dextrocardia may be a part of Kartagener syndrome or immotile cilia syndrome but is generally associated with normal cardiac anatomy. It is frequently detected by clinical examination with the heart sounds auscultated in the right chest and incidental chest radiograph demonstrating dextrocardia. In contrast, babies born with dextrocardia and visceral situs solitus frequently have associated congenital heart defects, ranging from simple septal defects to complex lesions such as L-transposition of the great arteries. The same is true for
paragraphs.heading: Bodily Arrangement and Situs

paragraphs.text: those neonates with situs inversus of their abdominal organs with levocardia (normal cardiac position with base to apex axis to the left), who almost always have associated cardiac defects.6 Situs ambiguous, with the liver in the midline, is seen in neonates with either bilateral right-sidedness or leftsidedness, also commonly referred to as heterotaxy syndrome or isomerism.4
paragraphs.heading: Bodily Arrangement and Situs

paragraphs.text: Isomerism is a clinical condition where there is a duplication of one side of the body across the vertical axis, leading to a bilateral symmetry or, in other words, loss of asymmetry between the right and left side of the body.5 Babies with bilateral right-sidedness (i.e., right isomerism, otherwise referred to as right atrial isomerism) tend to have asplenia, bilateral trilobed lungs, intestinal malrotation, extracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous return, frequent occurrence of left superior vena cava, co-localization of aorta and inferior vena cava on the same side, and atrioventricular septal defect7 (Figs. 77.2 and 77.3). In right isomerism, the coronary sinus, which lies posterior to the normal left atrium, is usually absent. Systemic venous return is also abnormal with the presence of bilateral superior vena cava. The left superior vena cava may enter directly into the roof of the left-sided morphologic right atrium or the coronary sinus, whereas the right superior vena cava generally enters the right atrium in a normal fashion.8 The right inferior vena cava is present, and there might be an additional left inferior vena cava. Another relatively common variety encountered in cardiac position is dextrocardia with an associated common atrium and a single atrioventricular valve, resulting in either a common ventricle or a large ventricular septal defect. Severe pulmonary stenosis or atresia is common in this particular defect.9 Right isomerism is more common in boys. Surgical palliation beginning as a neonate and terminating in a palliated univentricular circulation is the norm for over 80% of asplenia patients. Survival at 5 years in a live-born cohort of asplenia infants is 53% and is worse in those with stenotic pulmonary veins.10 Severe, life-threatening septic events are a considerable concern and daily, lifelong
paragraphs.heading: Bodily Arrangement and Situs

paragraphs.text: administration of a prophylactic antibiotic, as well as vaccinations against all capsulated bacteria (such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Hemophilus influenzae, which are opsonized in the normal spleen), to reduce the risk of bacterial sepsis is critically important.
paragraphs.heading: Bodily Arrangement and Situs

paragraphs.text: Babies with bilateral left-sidedness (i.e., left atrial isomerism) tend to have bilateral morphologic left atrial appendages, bilobed lungs, multiple splenic bodies, intestinal malrotation, interruption of the inferior vena cava with azygos continuation, heart block, atrioventricular septal defect, double outlet right ventricle, right or left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and anomalous pulmonary vein drainage that is often partial to the ipsilateral atrium and left superior vena cava (Fig. 77.4). In patients with polysplenia-associated left isomerism, the partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage is intracardiac; that means the right pulmonary vein may drain to the left-sided atrium or the left pulmonary vein may drain to the right atrium. In contrast, in asplenia-associated right isomerism, the pulmonary vein drainage is totally anomalous, and it is often extracardiac (means either supra- or infracardiac). Absence of the hepatic segment of the inferior vena cava (the socalled interrupted inferior vena cava) is an excellent clue to the presence of polysplenia or bilateral left-sidedness in a neonate with ambiguous abdominal situs (left isomerism). Because the baby has no true right atrium, the course of the inferior vena cava is often abnormal in almost 85% of the neonates with left isomerism. Drainage of the inferior vena cava is through the azygos or hemiazygos veins into the superior vena cava. With bilateral left atria, the pulmonary veins usually return to the heart in a bilateral fashion to their closest atrium (right-sided pulmonary veins return to the right-sided atrium). The presence of polysplenia is often associated with levocardia, normally related great arteries, a common atrium, and two ventricles with a ventricular septal defect.6 The pulmonary valve in these cases is usually normal. A quarter of fetuses with polysplenia may have bradyarrhythmia in utero, including sick sinus syndrome, sinus bradycardia (due to absence of a normal
paragraphs.heading: Bodily Arrangement and Situs

paragraphs.text: sinoatrial node, a right-sided atrial structure) and a compensatory low atrial rhythm originating from the inferiorly located coronary sinus. Patients with left isomerism tend to have atrioventricular block, intraventricular conduction delay, and atrioventricular nodal reentry tachycardia. On the other hand, patients with right isomerism tend to have atrial flutter, atrial tachycardia, junctional tachycardia, and ventricular tachycardia.11 Survival to birth in fetal bradyarrhythmia associated with polysplenia is nearly 80% in fetuses where termination is not chosen upon diagnosis. Survival at 5 years in a live-born cohort is 86% in polysplenia.12 Although the patient has multiple small spleens, splenic function can be either normal or abnormal regardless of the presence of Howell-Jolly bodies on blood smear, which may indicate hyposplenism.13 Assessment of splenic
paragraphs.heading: Bodily Arrangement and Situs

paragraphs.text: function and identification of the subset requiring daily prophylactic antibiotics are important prior to discharge home from the hospital.
paragraphs.heading: Bodily Arrangement and Situs

paragraphs.text: Univentricular palliation in patients with heterotaxy syndrome includes an initial stage where a unilateral or bilateral bidirectional Glenn shunt is done to divert the (unilateral or bilateral) venous return from the superior vena cava to the pulmonary circulation bypassing the right heart. In left isomerism with azygos continuation of the superior vena cava, this amounts to diversion of the entire systemic venous return barring the hepatic venous return directly to the lungs. Although this is advantageous in the short term
paragraphs.heading: Management Strategy

paragraphs.text: due to significant improvement of hypoxia after the surgery, early development of pulmonary arteriovenous malformations after Glenn shunt occurs due to the lack of hepatic factor X that inhibits pulmonary anomalous vasculogenesis. This leads to severe hypoxia upon late follow-up of these patients. Such malformations disappear when the secondstage palliation (namely, extracardiac conduit Fontan surgery) is completed where the hepatic veins are directed to the pulmonary circulation, thereby redirecting the hepatic factor X into the pulmonary circulation. Patients with heterotaxy syndromes and midline liver often have individual hepatic veins from different lobes draining separately into the atrium, sometimes far away from each other, and they need to be brought together while fashioning the lower inlet anastomosis of the extracardiac Fontan conduit.
paragraphs.heading: Management Strategy

paragraphs.text: Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are abnormal vascular malformations characterized by a network of malformed arteries and veins connected directly via a network of dysmorphic vessels (the nidus) that lack an intervening capillary bed.14 This leads to arteriovenous shunting and cardiac failure based on the severity of shunting. Although AVM can occur in any part of the body, neonatal presentation is usually seen with large malformations, the most significant of which is the cerebral vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation (VGAM).15 These AV malformations develop between the sixth and 11th weeks of gestation by the persistence of fistulae between embryonic pial arachnoidal arteries and veins.16 The feeder vessels in the AVM drain into the aberrantly persistent fetal median prosencephalic vein of Markowsky, an embryonic precursor of the vein of Galen.15 VGAM presents in the neonatal period with cardiac failure and hydrocephalus. Vein of Galen malformations can be classified as choroidal (type 1) or mural (type 2).17 The choroidal type usually presents in the neonatal period with high-output cardiac failure, macrocephaly with loud bruits, and dilated orbital veins due to multiple high-flow fistulas with less restriction of outflow.
paragraphs.heading: Arteriovenous Malformations

paragraphs.text: Even large VGAMs may not result in heart failure in the fetus, as the low resistance of the malformation is offset by the uteroplacental circulation.18 As systemic vascular resistance increases at birth, blood flow is progressively diverted into the malformation from the systemic circulation, resulting in systemic steal. Congestive heart failure, right heart dilation, lactic acidosis, persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, and diastolic runoff in the ascending aorta or arch on echocardiogram are clues to the diagnosis. Cranial bruit, a louder pulmonary component to the second heart sound, and a systolic ejection murmur of increased aortic and pulmonary artery flow are also typically present. The chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly. Early heart failure in VGAM is associated with worse outcomes.19 An
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: electrocardiogram (ECG) may demonstrate right ventricular hypertrophy and ST-T wave abnormalities due to coronary artery steal. In addition to flow reversal in the aorta, an echocardiogram will frequently demonstrate a dilated, noncompliant right ventricle with systemic or suprasystemic pulmonary artery pressures and a hyperdynamic left ventricle. Ductal flow may be right to left, resulting in significant cyanosis. Diagnosis is confirmed with CT or MRI.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The main goal of treating a VGAM is to reduce as much of the blood flow through the VGAM as possible so that the blood supply to the brain is restored while stabilizing the systemic cardiac output.18 For initial stabilization, milrinone and inhaled nitric oxide have been utilized along with loop diuretics.16 Medical management fails in about half of the patients, necessitating an interventional procedure.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Endovascular embolization has replaced surgery as the mainstay of treatment of vein of Galen malformations.20 Most hospitals prefer transarterial embolization. This technique is particularly helpful when the number of arterial feeders is low. If there are many small arterial pedicles, a combination of the transvenous and transarterial embolization (kissing microcatheter technique) can be employed to improve the success rate.21 Over the years, the outcomes have improved, although a mild developmental delay is expected in severe cases.22 Earlier presentation has worse outcomes, as neonates showed the worst mortality rate of 52% following endovascular treatment, with only 36% of survivors being neurologically normal.16 In patients with less severe symptoms that can be managed medically, survival after treatment in the age group of 5 months to 2 years increases to more than 90%, with 78% of survivors classified as neurologically normal.16
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Neonatal cardiomyopathy is comprised of diseases of the heart muscle of the newborn in which the myocardium is affected in the absence of primary abnormalities of the valves, great vessels, or the septum.23 Cardiomyopathy refers to a diverse group of myocardial diseases with multiple causes. Although these are rare disorders, accounting for only approximately 1% of childhood cardiac diseases, these conditions contribute to 10% of mortality in childhood.24 In 1995, the World Health Organization classified the phenotypes of cardiomyopathies into hypertrophic, dilated, restrictive, and mixed types.25 The American Heart Association, in 2006, classified cardiomyopathies into two major groups based on predominant organ involvement and etiology as primary (genetic, mixed, or acquired) or secondary (Figs. 77.5 and 77.6, respectively).25,26 A phenotype-genotype–based MOGE(S) classification of cardiomyopathies was proposed by the World Heart Federation in 2013.27
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Diseases: Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis

paragraphs.text: This classification is based on five characteristics of cardiomyopathic disorders: morphofunctional state (M), organ involvement (O), genetic inheritance (G), etiologic annotation (E), and functional state (S) according to the functional class (Fig. 77.7). Although the MOGE(S) classification has several advantages, including maximal description of the disease from clinical and genetic points, the downside is that this classification is not based on the clinical diagnostic criteria of cardiomyopathies and the paucity of genetic testing in most clinical centers. Primary cardiomyopathies are those solely or predominantly confined to heart muscle. Secondary cardiomyopathies develop myocardial damage following systemic or multi-organ disorders (Fig. 77.6). Myocarditis, an inflammatory process affecting the myocardium, is classified as acute or chronic. Myocarditis may result in either a dilated (common) or restrictive (rare) cardiomyopathy. About half of the acute myocarditis cases are infectious in origin.28 There are reports of newborns developing myocarditis and cardiomyopathy following COVID-19 infection.29
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Diseases: Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis

paragraphs.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is characterized by enlargement and dilation of one or both ventricles associated with impaired contractility as defined by a reduction in left ventricular ejection fraction to less than 40% (Fig. 77.8).30 The patient’s cardiac output (heart rate × stroke volume) is often decreased due to a reduction in stroke volume as the ventricular filling pressures are increased. Total ventricular mass is increased, but the chamber volume is disproportionately enlarged. This ventricular enlargement can be due to either a primary cardiomyopathic process or secondary to left ventricular failure. This can be associated with both systolic and diastolic dysfunction. Myocardial remodeling causes a reduction in systolic function. This progressively leads to an increase in both end-systolic and enddiastolic volumes. These neonates present with symptoms of poor cardiac output, including pallor, irritability, poor feeding, respiratory distress, and diaphoresis. Physical signs include tachypnea, tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, and hepatomegaly. Decompensated infants present with shock
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Diseases: Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis

paragraphs.text: and cardiovascular collapse. Cardiac auscultation often reveals muffled heart sounds with a gallop rhythm (S3, S4). Occasionally, a murmur of mitral regurgitation can be auscultated. Arrhythmias, although rare, are an ominous, often undetected presentation. The ECG in a patient with DCM shows flattening of the T waves with possible depression of the ST segments. The chest x-ray often shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary edema. Atrioventricular block may be present, particularly in patients carrying mutations of the lamin A/C gene (LMNA) and in patients with DCM secondary to congenital complete atrioventricular block and neonatal lupus.31 Echocardiogram is diagnostic, illustrating dilation of the ventricle(s) and poor cardiac contractility. Cardiac MRI is increasingly part of the diagnostic workup, often demonstrating myocardial fibrosis and scarring. MRI has become useful in differentiating DCM from acute myocarditis. An extensive family history is essential when evaluating neonates. Idiopathic DCM is associated with a familial component in 20% to 48% of patients.32 An autosomal dominant pattern is the most predominant one, although X-linked, autosomal recessive and mitochondrial inheritance are also described. Initial management of these patients involves rescue from circulatory collapse using oxygen supplementation, ventilatory support, sedation, and vascular access. Long-term management targets neurohormonal activation during heart failure, including spironolactone and loop diuretics, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or receptor blockers, and inotropes for acute decompensation. There are conflicting data in neonates and infants regarding the use of beta-blockers in the management of DCM, with many experienced institutions continuing to add carvedilol to augment medical management.33 Beta-blockers suppress the excessive sympathetic activity contributing to cardiac failure. The primary goal of therapy is to relieve symptoms and prolong survival. Often, these patients may require the use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and/or ventricular assist device
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Diseases: Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis

paragraphs.text: (VAD) as a bridge to recovery or transplant. As mechanical support technology has improved, VADs have demonstrated improvement in survival over ECMO.34 All forms of mechanical support have a high incidence of adverse event rates, particularly hemorrhage and thrombosis events in children under 10 kg.35
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Diseases: Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis

paragraphs.text: Certain cardiac conditions clinically present with echocardiographic features indistinguishable from DCM. These conditions may be amenable for correction if they are identified early and appropriate treatment is initiated. Among these conditions, it is important to exclude the anomalous origin of left coronary artery from pulmonary artery when considering the diagnosis of DCM. In such patients, high fetal pulmonary vascular resistance maintains coronary perfusion in the early neonatal period. However, following birth, a fall in pulmonary artery pressures leads to myocardial ischemia, exaggerated by a steal of blood from the myocardium to the pulmonary artery by a reversal of flow, worsening the ischemia in due course.
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Diseases: Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis

paragraphs.text: Another lesion that masquerades as DCM is severe left ventricular outflow obstruction (Fig. 77.9). Stenosis such as aortic stenosis is easy to detect; however, distant obstructions such as coarctation or aortic thrombosis may be missed on echocardiography. A careful clinical examination of femoral artery pulses often clinches the diagnosis.36
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Diseases: Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis

paragraphs.text: Fetal or neonatal tachyarrhythmias may present as DCM, especially when the heart rates are not high enough to warrant the clinician’s attention. Some of the most common tachyarrhythmias that mimic a DCM include the permanent form of junctional reciprocating tachycardia (a reentrant tachycardia that uses a decremental conducting accessory pathway), ectopic atrial tachycardia, and atrial flutter.
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Diseases: Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis

paragraphs.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is characterized by increased cardiac muscle mass that generally affects the left ventricle and is not solely explained by abnormal
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Diseases: Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis

paragraphs.text: loading conditions.37 The left ventricular mass/volume ratio is increased, resulting in a left ventricular cavity that is decreased in size because of thickening of the muscle, particularly in the interventricular septum, resulting in dynamic outflow obstruction. The systolic function of the heart is preserved or increased in this disorder when assessed by echocardiogram. The patient’s clinical picture is generally dominated by diastolic dysfunction, with elevated ventricular filling pressures. Infants who have HCM present with symptoms of congestive heart failure, including tachypnea, poor feeding, and growth failure.38 The diagnosis is frequently made during screening because of a known immediate family member with HCM or an unexplained early death in the family. Occasionally, a near-miss sudden death episode with arrhythmia is the sentinel event. Mutations in sarcomeric genes are the most important cause of HCM in
paragraphs.heading: O

paragraphs.text: both adults and in children (40%–60% of cases).39 HCM can also be due to inherited errors of metabolism (e.g., glycogen storage diseases [GSDs], lysosomal storage diseases, and fatty acid oxidation disorders), neuromuscular diseases, and mitochondrial diseases. The ECG often shows left ventricular hypertrophy with ST and T changes that may be consistent with the strain. The echocardiogram is generally diagnostic for this disorder and is helpful in assessing overall myocardial thickness, chamber dimensions, and systolic and diastolic performance of the ventricle. Cardiac MRI with myocardial T1 mapping can demonstrate myocardial fibrosis and scarring even early in the time course.38 The primary goals of management of these patients are similar to those of DCM—providing symptomatic relief and prolonging survival. Medical management includes the use of beta-blockers to augment diastolic filling time, thereby increasing the
paragraphs.heading: O

paragraphs.text: left ventricular end-diastolic volume and relieving dynamic outflow obstruction. Diuretics are counterproductive because they decrease the patient’s overall blood volume, thereby decreasing the ventricular preload which, in turn, reduces stroke volume and cardiac output. A reduction in ventricular cavity size could also increase the outflow tract obstruction. Systemic vasodilators, such as ACE inhibitors, and inodilators such as milrinone increase the ventricular outflow gradient and therefore should be avoided. Negative inotropes such as calcium channel blockers may be
paragraphs.heading: O

paragraphs.text: used judiciously, as the neonatal myocardium is particularly reliant on calcium. The neonatal heart has poor ventricular compliance due to the narrow Frank-Starling curve. This impairs the ability of the neonatal heart to alter cardiac output based on stroke volume, preload, and afterload, leading to an excessive reliance on heart rate to maintain cardiac output.40 The prognosis of HCM in this age group is rather poor compared to older children. Infants with HCM have a 2-year mortality of 30%. Death is rare in older children.41 Neonates with underlying inborn errors of metabolism and
paragraphs.heading: O

paragraphs.text: malformation syndromes have a poorer prognosis when compared to neonates with idiopathic infantile HCM.42
paragraphs.heading: O

paragraphs.text: Another form of HCM seen in the neonatal period is the myopathy of infants of diabetic mothers, which carries an excellent prognosis with complete resolution within the first 6 months of life, and steroid-induced HCM, which typically resolves after discontinuation of the steroids.43,44 It is interesting to note that infants with hyperinsulinism severe enough to require pancreatectomy are at particular risk of developing HCM.45 Dexamethasone and methylprednisone both have an increased risk of developing HCM in the early newborn period in premature infants.46 Therefore the American Academy of Pediatrics cautioned against treatment with dexamethasone for infants with birth weights less than 1500 g (very low birth weight) and recommended limiting its use to exceptional clinical circumstances.47 Left ventricular noncompaction is an imaging-based diagnosis referring to prominent left ventricular trabeculae, a thin compacted layer, and deep recesses continuous with the left ventricular cavity.48 Noncompaction may be associated with muscular dystrophies, Barth syndrome, or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or DCM. Several genes overlap, with known mutations affecting the conduction system and contributing to prolongation of the QT interval and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Individual treatment plans should be tailored toward associated arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy risks.
paragraphs.heading: O

paragraphs.text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is the least common phenotype of cardiomyopathy, causing only up to 3% of cardiomyopathies diagnosed during childhood.49 The European Society of Cardiology characterizes RCM as a myocardial disease defined by impaired ventricular filling accompanied by normal/reduced diastolic volumes with near-normal myocardial thickness and ejection fraction.50 Reduced active relaxation and increased muscle stiffness lead to a rise in pressure within the ventricles during diastole, reducing the filling and leading to a reduction in stroke volume. Although systolic function is preserved in RCM in
paragraphs.heading: O

paragraphs.text: early stages, contractility is subnormal. Neonates with this disorder present with signs and symptoms of congestive heart failure and pulmonary hypertension. The ECG often shows conduction abnormalities and evidence of ischemia at faster heart rates. The echocardiogram shows normal or small ventricles with dilation of both atria and signs of right ventricular pressure load. Although uncommon in neonates, it should be differentiated from constrictive pericarditis, as the conditions could have similar presentation. Cardiac transplantation is the definitive cure, and mechanical circulatory support may be necessary to buy time for a transplant. The most common pediatric long-term circulatory support device is the pneumatically driven, pulsatile Berlin Heart EXCOR device. This is the only long-term device approved for use in neonates and infants approved in Europe and the United States.51 Median transplant-free survival for newly diagnosed RCM is very poor. In the Pediatric Cardiomyopathy Registry analysis, freedom from death or transplant was 48% at 1 year in patients with pure RCM.52
paragraphs.heading: O

paragraphs.text: The approach to neonates with suspected cardiomyopathy or myocarditis must include a methodical approach to the diagnosis and a level of support appropriate for their clinical symptoms. Specialized early referral to heart failure and cardiac transplant teams is critical in long-term management of these infants. Endomyocardial biopsy can guide therapy and help in defining the prognosis by identifying pathologic features but is not routinely recommended due to the related risks including tamponade and lethal arrhythmia. The improvement in MRI technology has permitted noninvasive diagnosis by cardiac magnetic resonance. Use of late gadolinium enhancement patterns in the myocardium has allowed determination of the etiology of heart failure.53 Evidence of active inflammation or immune suppression can be treated with intravenously administered immunoglobulin,
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis and Treatment

paragraphs.text: although its role in the treatment of myocarditis, especially in neonates and infants, remains to be fully validated.54 The prognosis is often good if the baby can be managed through an episode of myocarditis. In contrast, if a biopsy shows endocardial fibroelastosis or the echocardiogram shows endocardial thickening, then the likelihood of recovery of myocardial function is very poor.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis and Treatment

paragraphs.text: A pericardial effusion is present when there is increased fluid within the existing pericardial space. This fluid can be serous, sanguineous, serosanguineous, purulent, or lymphatic in nature. The most common cause of pericardial effusion is iatrogenic and is mainly due to central venous catheters.55 Pericardial effusion is also seen in neonates who have fetal hydrops due to a variety of causes. Pericardial effusions can also be the result of open-heart surgery, specifically repair of atrial septal defects or ECMO catheter insertion.56 Pneumopericardium is a complication of mechanical ventilation and can have hemodynamic effects similar to those of fluid. If the pericardial fluid accumulates gradually, the intrapericardial pressure remains low, and symptoms are generally absent until the effusion becomes large enough to cause tamponade. Rapid accumulation of a pericardial effusion, regardless of etiology, can result in pericardial tamponade, even with small volumes.
paragraphs.heading: Pericardial Diseases

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of pericardial tamponade should be suspected in any baby with early signs of poor cardiac output, including tachycardia and poor perfusion. Pulsus paradoxus, an exaggerated fall in blood pressure with inspiration, is easiest to observe in neonates with arterial lines for continuous blood pressure monitoring. A dramatic increase in heart size on a chest radiograph supports the clinical diagnosis. Intrapericardial air is usually obvious on the radiograph and can be differentiated from mediastinal air because it encircles the heart. Echocardiography is the best way to establish the diagnosis of pericardial effusion and to assess the physiological impact of the effusion. In echocardiography, an early sign of tamponade is systolic right atrial collapse, whereas a diastolic right ventricular collapse has high specificity and a plethoric inferior vena cava with minimal respiratory variation has high sensitivity. The respiratory variation of tricuspid and mitral inflow can exceed 30%, further confirming the clinical picture.57 The size of the pericardiac effusion is estimated by semiquantitative echocardiographic assessment. This is defined as the maximum perpendicular distance between the two layers at end-diastole, as measured in the subxiphoid view.58 Pericardiocentesis by the subxiphoid approach can be used to drain fluid or air to help alleviate symptoms. If fluid or air returns, a small catheter can be placed percutaneously or surgically and left to continuously drain the fluid.
paragraphs.heading: Pericardial Diseases

paragraphs.text: Pericarditis is extremely rare in the neonatal period and usually is associated with myocarditis and/or systemic inflammation. Treatment is symptomatic and consists of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Prognosis is
paragraphs.heading: Pericardial Diseases

paragraphs.text: generally good, but this condition can lead to constrictive pericarditis.
paragraphs.heading: Pericardial Diseases

paragraphs.text: Primary cardiac and mediastinal tumors are rare at all ages and even less common in infants and children. Most of the cardiac tumors reported are benign, with rhabdomyomas, fibromas, and teratomas contributing to the majority. Presentation of such tumors depends on the size and location of the mass, as they have a propensity to cause inflow or outflow tract obstruction and arrhythmias.59,60 Rhabdomyomas are the most common tumor type in this age group but are, in fact, hamartomas, whereas malignant cardiac or mediastinal tumors are extremely rare.61 Clinical manifestation of these tumors varies from incidental findings on echocardiogram to those causing life-threatening cardiac events.
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Tumors

paragraphs.text: In 30% to 91% of cases, cardiac rhabdomyomas, especially when multiple in numbers, are associated with tuberous sclerosis.61 Depending upon the size and placement, rhabdomyomas can interfere with ventricular filling or emptying. When they are located near the atrioventricular valves, the tissue can serve as a bypass tract and mimic the features of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.62 Confirmation by myocardial biopsy in a symptom-free neonate is not necessary, especially when the neurocutaneous features of tuberous sclerosis are present. Rhabdomyomas lose their mitotic potential postnatally, causing tumor regression.63 Hence, surgical excision is not necessary unless the tumor is obstructing the flow or is discrete or pedunculated enough to allow excision.
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Tumors

paragraphs.text: Other rare tumors that can occur in the neonate include myocardial hemangioma, fibromas, and pericardial teratomas.64 Myocardial hemangiomas are tumors with dense capillary beds that can have connections to the coronary arteries. They are on the epicardial surface with intrusion into the myocardium.65 Hemangiomas can cause subpulmonary stenosis if they are located in the right ventricular outflow tract. Small hamartomas cause histiocytoid or oncocytic cardiomyopathy which is associated with severe and persistent ventricular arrhythmias. Usually, such tumors are subendocardial in location and comprised of pathognomonic nests of foamy appearing myocytes resembling macrophages.66 In infants with refractory arrhythmias, electrophysiological mapping and ablation may be required. Myocardial fibroma can be located in the myocardium or on the atrial wall or can involve the mitral valve and cause obstruction. Fibromas can also disrupt the conduction system and contribute to ventricular arrhythmias. Intrapericardial teratoma is a benign tumor attached to the base of the aorta. It is associated with mediastinal compression and pericardial effusion in the fetus, neonate, or young infant. Successful excision of intrapericardial teratoma has been reported, although large tumors can cause fetal death. Atrial myxomas have not been reported in the neonatal period. Surgical excision is required if there is obstruction to the inflow or outflow of the heart.
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Tumors

paragraphs.text: Associated arrhythmias should be treated with antiarrhythmics, as described in the other sections of this book. There is an increasing role for cardiac MRI in distinguishing cardiac tumors, thereby avoiding the need for invasive biopsy.65
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Tumors

paragraphs.text: Vascular rings are anomalies that result from abnormal development of the aortic arch complex and cause compression of the trachea, esophagus, or both. Vascular rings can be complete (double aortic arch or right aortic arch with left ligament) or incomplete (innominate artery compression and pulmonary slings).67 The first description of the anatomy of a double aortic arch was done in 1737 by the anatomist Hommel.68
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: Embryological basis of the vascular ring lies in the principle that, during development, the vascular double arch system develops with complete involution of the first, second,
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: and fifth aortic arches followed by appropriate development of the remaining arches.67,69 During normal aortic development, the third arches develop into the common carotid arteries. The left fourth arch becomes the aortic arch, and the right fourth arch involutes. The sixth arch on the left side becomes the left pulmonary artery and the ductus arteriosus, whereas on the right side it becomes the right pulmonary artery.
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: Persistence of both right and left fourth branchial arches due to an arrest in regression of a unilateral arch results in a double aortic arch, with each of the arches passing above the main stem bronchus on the right and left side and joining together behind the trachea to form the descending aorta. These result in compression of the trachea, causing symptoms such as respiratory distress and stridor. In most cases of double aortic arch, the right arch is the dominant one, with the left arch being smaller (Figs. 77.10 to 77.13).67
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: Initial screening of a neonate with respiratory distress due to stridor using echocardiography may provide the first clue to the presence of a vascular ring.
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: If the left fourth arch involutes, it results in a right aortic arch, but that does not lead to formation of a ring. If the ligamentum arises from the descending aorta on the right side and attaches to the pulmonary artery on the left, it forms a complete vascular ring with compression of the trachea between the arch on the right side and ligamentum between the descending aorta and pulmonary artery on the left side. Patients with a right aortic arch and a left ligamentum may also have a Kommerell diverticulum at the origin of the left subclavian artery from the descending aorta (Fig. 77.14).70 This diverticulum, a remnant of the left dorsal arch where the left aberrant subclavian artery originates, could cause posterior compression of the esophagus.
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: Other relatively uncommon anomalies contributing to complete vascular rings include a circumflex aorta and cervical aortic arch with airway compression. A circumflex aorta is defined as an ipsilateral aortic arch with contralateral descending thoracic aorta (Fig. 77.15). In this condition, the aortic arch, after crossing the ipsilateral bronchus, turns around behind the trachea and esophagus and descends on the contralateral side. A ductus arteriosus or ligamentum arteriosum from the proximal descending aorta completes the vascular ring. Unlike double arch or right arch with aberrant left subclavian artery, which can be surgically corrected by a simple thoracotomy procedure, a circumflex aorta requires descending aortic reimplantation to the posterior wall of ascending aorta on extracorporeal circulation to relieve the airway obstruction.71,72
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: The last condition that we describe under the aortic vascular ring is the cervical arch, which supposedly originates from persisting third aortic arch remnants (Fig. 77.16). The arch gives off multiple separate branches to the head and neck, including both external and internal carotid arteries. In addition, the vertebral artery may originate separately from the subclavian. An anomalous duct or ligament completes the vascular ring in this instance, as well. The condition is diagnosed when the arch extends above the thoracic inlet, which is guarded by the superior end of manubrium sterni and first rib. The condition is characterized by prominent neck pulsations clinically, and imaging confirms the diagnosis.
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: A pulmonary artery sling is caused when the origin of all or part of the left pulmonary artery comes from the right pulmonary artery (Fig. 77.17). The embryonic origin of a pulmonary artery sling occurs when the developing left lung captures its arterial supply from derivatives of the right sixth arch through capillaries caudal, rather than cephalad, to the developing tracheobronchial tree.67 The left pulmonary artery passes around the right main stem bronchus and courses between the trachea and esophagus, forming a “sling.” This might be associated with circumferential cartilage rings in the trachea with absence of the membranous portion posteriorly, the so-called ring-sling complex.73
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: Innominate artery compression syndrome is caused by the anterior compression of the trachea anteriorly by the
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: innominate artery. The exact etiology of this syndrome is not well understood. The innominate artery in some children originates more posteriorly in the left aortic arch, and as it courses posteriorly and superiorly anterior to the trachea, it causes compression.
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: An aberrant subclavian artery (left aortic arch with retro-esophageal right subclavian artery) results from the disappearance of the right fourth aortic arch. The right subclavian artery arises from the descending aorta, coursing superiorly behind the esophagus. This is the most common arch anomaly, seen in 0.5% of the general population. Most infants are asymptomatic, and the diagnosis is suspected on an incidental echocardiogram. Barium swallow is usually diagnostic, showing posterior indentation on the esophagus. The aberrant right subclavian is rarely the true cause of dysphagia, hence the label dysphagia lusoria.74
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: A right aortic arch with retro-esophageal left subclavian artery is usually associated with other conotruncal abnormalities.
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Rings and Slings

paragraphs.text: Many children with vascular rings presenting within their first year of life require surgery. These infants commonly present with respiratory difficulties (e.g., stridor or wheezing), recurrent pulmonary infections, and/or difficulty feeding.67 Infants may hold their heads hyperextended, thereby decreasing the obstruction. In older infants and children, the presenting features might be dysphagia with solid foods. Children with innominate artery compression may present with apnea. The diagnostic evaluation includes chest radiography, echocardiogram, barium swallow studies, CT
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: angiogram (CTA), and cardiac MRI. CTA enables high-resolution evaluation of vascular anomalies and tracheal compression. Three-dimensional reconstruction of the CT scan provides high-quality images that would enable planning of surgical repair. CTA often provides the final diagnosis and is considered the gold standard diagnostic test, although MRI is gaining more acceptance and sensitivity.75
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Surgery is indicated in all symptomatic vascular rings. Delayed treatment may result in sudden death or further
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: tracheobronchial damage. Willis J. Potts at the Children’s Memorial Hospital in Chicago was the first to describe a successful repair of the pulmonary artery sling in 1954.76 All patients referred for surgery should have the airway evaluated for the site of tracheal stenosis and evaluation of cartilage rings. Bronchoscopy may be necessary to diagnose additional tracheal pathology, including tracheomalacia and bronchomalacia.69 The nondominant arch is divided in the case of a double aortic arch. Coarctation and other associated anomalies should be ruled out before referral for surgery. The ligamentum is divided and ligated in the case of a right arch and a left ligamentum. If a Kommerell
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: diverticulum is 1.5 to 2 times the size of the left subclavian artery, it should be resected.70 Compression of the trachea by the innominate artery may be treated by reimplanting the innominate artery. A pulmonary artery sling is corrected by reimplantation of the left pulmonary artery into the main pulmonary artery, anterior to the trachea. An aberrant subclavian artery requires treatment only if associated with aneurysm at the origin of the subclavian artery.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Neonatal Marfan syndrome (nMFS) is a rare condition and is genotypically and phenotypically quite distinct from the typical Marfan syndrome. The syndrome carries a poorer prognosis, as the cardiovascular complications associated with this disorder are associated with significant morbidity and mortality.77 Ninety percent of patients with nMFS die within the first year of life, signifying the poor prognosis. The diagnosis of nMFS, because of its clinical and phenotypic variability, is made following the criteria of skeletal, ocular, cardiovascular, cutaneous, neurologic, and pulmonary manifestations, as well as family history. Cardiac pathology is more severe in nMFS, with severe mitral and/ or tricuspid valve insufficiency leading to congestive cardiac failure from infancy. Aortic root dilatation and regurgitation are more common in classical Marfan syndrome.78 Other features such as joint contractures, megalocornea, iridodonesis, ectopia lentis, redundant loose skin, and crumpled ears are more common in the neonatal form compared to the classical form.
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Marfan Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Most severe cases are caused by a sporadic mutation in a single germ cell of one parent. Mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15, encoding the protein fibrillin-1, cause Marfan syndrome. Mutations associated with nMFS have been consistently reported in exons 24 to 32 of the same chromosome. Mutations in the region of exons 25 and 26 are associated with a shorter survival in children diagnosed with nMFS before the age of 1 year.78 Genetic testing to
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Marfan Syndrome

paragraphs.text: exclude Loeys-Dietz syndrome may also be indicated in the neonate presenting with physical findings of connective tissue abnormalities. This exclusion may be recognized clinically, as infants with Loeys-Dietz syndrome will have a bifid uvula and, more critically, severe dilation of the aorta and cerebral arteries, leading to earlier pathology and rupture. Surgery is often required early in these infants because of persistent heart failure and the risk of death from aortic rupture. In a rare case, quadruple valve replacement has been reported.
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Marfan Syndrome

paragraphs.text: The prevalence of congenital heart disease (CHD) in premature infants born at 25 to 32 weeks’ gestational age (116/1000 births of similar gestational age) is reported as significantly higher than the prevalence of CHDs in term neonates (6–10/1000 births).79 Compared with extremely premature neonates without CHD, those with severe CHD had more than sevenfold increased odds of mortality.79 When compared with term infants, low birth weight/premature infants were more likely to have pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect, complete atrioventricular septal defect, coarctation of the aorta, tetralogy of Fallot, and pulmonary valve stenosis. Fewer low birth weight/preterm infants had pulmonary atresia and intact ventricular septum, transposition of the great arteries, and single ventricle. Perioperative management of these high-risk infants must take into account the patient’s small size, the clinical implications of prematurity, intrauterine growth restriction, associated extracardiac anomalies, and issues related to anesthesia, surgery, and cardiopulmonary bypass.80
paragraphs.heading: Heart Disease

paragraphs.text: Comorbidities with surgical and medical management of persistent ductus arteriosus in the preterm infant have sparked interest in catheter-based closure.81 It has been noted that severe CHD was not associated with neonatal
paragraphs.heading: Heart Disease

paragraphs.text: brain injury, necrotizing enterocolitis, or retinopathy of prematurity. On the contrary, the risk for bronchopulmonary dysplasia was increased.82
paragraphs.heading: Heart Disease

paragraphs.text: The combination of low birth weight, prematurity, and CHD makes the management of these patients challenging, and on certain occasions palliative care is appropriate.83 It is unclear whether a strategy of medical management and deferment of surgical intervention is beneficial over more expeditious intervention.

### ANANTHA KRISHNAN HARIJITH, TARA SUDHADEVI, AND KOTHANDAM SIVAKUMAR

### Cardiac Malposition and Abnormalities of Abdominal Situs

### Bodily Arrangement and Situs

The development of morphologically right-sided structures on one side of the body and morphologically left-sided structures on the other side is termed lateralization or situs. The normal disposition of organs in which right-sided structures are on the right side of the body, and vice versa, is known as situs solitus.1,2 The term viscero-atrial situs is often used to refer to the situs of the viscera, or noncardiac organs, and atria when their situs are in agreement. In normal atrial arrangement, or atrial situs solitus, the left atrium is on the left side and right atrium is on the right side. In atrial situs inversus, the left atrium is on the right side and the right atrium is on the left side. The relationship between the pulmonary artery and the bronchus is asymmetric. The right lung anatomically has an eparterial bronchus (i.e., one that branches superior to the first lobar division of the pulmonary artery), in contrast to the left-sided lung, which has a hyparterial bronchus (i.e., one that branches inferior to the first lobar division of the respective pulmonary artery) (Fig. 77.1).3

Visceral situs solitus occurs when the abdominal organs are lateralized normally with the spleen and stomach on the left side and liver on the right side. Situs solitus implies normal viscero-atrial concordance, but there need not be atrioventricular or ventriculo-arterial concordance. A discordance at any level could cause clinical problems. A failure in the normal left-right asymmetry comes under a spectrum of laterality disturbances and is known as heterotaxia.4 Physical examination assisted by imaging studies such as ultrasound scan of the abdomen, computed tomography (CT) scan, or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) helps determine the lateralization of internal organs.

### Arteriovenous Malformations

Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are abnormal vascular malformations characterized by a network of malformed arteries and veins connected directly via a network of dysmorphic vessels (the nidus) that lack an intervening capillary bed.14 This leads to arteriovenous shunting and cardiac failure based on the severity of shunting. Although AVM can occur in any part of the body, neonatal presentation is usually seen with large malformations, the most significant of which is the cerebral vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation (VGAM).15 These AV malformations develop between the sixth and 11th weeks of gestation by the persistence of fistulae between embryonic pial arachnoidal arteries and veins.16 The feeder vessels in the AVM drain into the aberrantly persistent fetal median prosencephalic vein of Markowsky, an embryonic precursor of the vein of Galen.15 VGAM presents in the neonatal period with cardiac failure and hydrocephalus. Vein of Galen malformations can be classified as choroidal (type 1) or mural (type 2).17 The choroidal type usually presents in the neonatal period with high-output cardiac failure, macrocephaly with loud bruits, and dilated orbital veins due to multiple high-flow fistulas with less restriction of outflow.

### Diagnosis

Even large VGAMs may not result in heart failure in the fetus, as the low resistance of the malformation is offset by the uteroplacental circulation.18 As systemic vascular resistance increases at birth, blood flow is progressively diverted into the malformation from the systemic circulation, resulting in systemic steal. Congestive heart failure, right heart dilation, lactic acidosis, persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, and diastolic runoff in the ascending aorta or arch on echocardiogram are clues to the diagnosis. Cranial bruit, a louder pulmonary component to the second heart sound, and a systolic ejection murmur of increased aortic and pulmonary artery flow are also typically present. The chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly. Early heart failure in VGAM is associated with worse outcomes.19 An

electrocardiogram (ECG) may demonstrate right ventricular hypertrophy and ST-T wave abnormalities due to coronary artery steal. In addition to flow reversal in the aorta, an echocardiogram will frequently demonstrate a dilated, noncompliant right ventricle with systemic or suprasystemic pulmonary artery pressures and a hyperdynamic left ventricle. Ductal flow may be right to left, resulting in significant cyanosis. Diagnosis is confirmed with CT or MRI.

### Treatment

The main goal of treating a VGAM is to reduce as much of the blood flow through the VGAM as possible so that the blood supply to the brain is restored while stabilizing the systemic cardiac output.18 For initial stabilization, milrinone and inhaled nitric oxide have been utilized along with loop diuretics.16 Medical management fails in about half of the patients, necessitating an interventional procedure.

Endovascular embolization has replaced surgery as the mainstay of treatment of vein of Galen malformations.20 Most hospitals prefer transarterial embolization. This technique is particularly helpful when the number of arterial feeders is low. If there are many small arterial pedicles, a combination of the transvenous and transarterial embolization (kissing microcatheter technique) can be employed to improve the success rate.21 Over the years, the outcomes have improved, although a mild developmental delay is expected in severe cases.22 Earlier presentation has worse outcomes, as neonates showed the worst mortality rate of 52% following endovascular treatment, with only 36% of survivors being neurologically normal.16 In patients with less severe symptoms that can be managed medically, survival after treatment in the age group of 5 months to 2 years increases to more than 90%, with 78% of survivors classified as neurologically normal.16

### Myocardial Diseases: Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis

Neonatal cardiomyopathy is comprised of diseases of the heart muscle of the newborn in which the myocardium is affected in the absence of primary abnormalities of the valves, great vessels, or the septum.23 Cardiomyopathy refers to a diverse group of myocardial diseases with multiple causes. ### Pericardial Diseases

A pericardial effusion is present when there is increased fluid within the existing pericardial space. This fluid can be serous, sanguineous, serosanguineous, purulent, or lymphatic in nature. The most common cause of pericardial effusion is iatrogenic and is mainly due to central venous catheters.55 Pericardial effusion is also seen in neonates who have fetal hydrops due to a variety of causes. Pericardial effusions can also be the result of open-heart surgery, specifically repair of atrial septal defects or ECMO catheter insertion.56 Pneumopericardium is a complication of mechanical ventilation and can have hemodynamic effects similar to those of fluid. If the pericardial fluid accumulates gradually, the intrapericardial pressure remains low, and symptoms are generally absent until the effusion becomes large enough to cause tamponade. Rapid accumulation of a pericardial effusion, regardless of etiology, can result in pericardial tamponade, even with small volumes.

The diagnosis of pericardial tamponade should be suspected in any baby with early signs of poor cardiac output, including tachycardia and poor perfusion. Pulsus paradoxus, an exaggerated fall in blood pressure with inspiration, is easiest to observe in neonates with arterial lines for continuous blood pressure monitoring. A dramatic increase in heart size on a chest radiograph supports the clinical diagnosis. Intrapericardial air is usually obvious on the radiograph and can be differentiated from mediastinal air because it encircles the heart. Echocardiography is the best way to establish the diagnosis of pericardial effusion and to assess the physiological impact of the effusion. In echocardiography, an early sign of tamponade is systolic right atrial collapse, whereas a diastolic right ventricular collapse has high specificity and a plethoric inferior vena cava with minimal respiratory variation has high sensitivity. The respiratory variation of tricuspid and mitral inflow can exceed 30%, further confirming the clinical picture.57 The size of the pericardiac effusion is estimated by semiquantitative echocardiographic assessment. This is defined as the maximum perpendicular distance between the two layers at end-diastole, as measured in the subxiphoid view.58 Pericardiocentesis by the subxiphoid approach can be used to drain fluid or air to help alleviate symptoms. If fluid or air returns, a small catheter can be placed percutaneously or surgically and left to continuously drain the fluid.

Pericarditis is extremely rare in the neonatal period and usually is associated with myocarditis and/or systemic inflammation. Treatment is symptomatic and consists of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Prognosis is

generally good, but this condition can lead to constrictive pericarditis.

### Cardiac Tumors

Primary cardiac and mediastinal tumors are rare at all ages and even less common in infants and children. Most of the cardiac tumors reported are benign, with rhabdomyomas, fibromas, and teratomas contributing to the majority. Presentation of such tumors depends on the size and location of the mass, as they have a propensity to cause inflow or outflow tract obstruction and arrhythmias.59,60 Rhabdomyomas are the most common tumor type in this age group but are, in fact, hamartomas, whereas malignant cardiac or mediastinal tumors are extremely rare.61 Clinical manifestation of these tumors varies from incidental findings on echocardiogram to those causing life-threatening cardiac events.

In 30% to 91% of cases, cardiac rhabdomyomas, especially when multiple in numbers, are associated with tuberous sclerosis.61 Depending upon the size and placement, rhabdomyomas can interfere with ventricular filling or emptying. When they are located near the atrioventricular valves, the tissue can serve as a bypass tract and mimic the features of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.62 Confirmation by myocardial biopsy in a symptom-free neonate is not necessary, especially when the neurocutaneous features of tuberous sclerosis are present. Rhabdomyomas lose their mitotic potential postnatally, causing tumor regression.63 Hence, surgical excision is not necessary unless the tumor is obstructing the flow or is discrete or pedunculated enough to allow excision.

Other rare tumors that can occur in the neonate include myocardial hemangioma, fibromas, and pericardial teratomas.64 Myocardial hemangiomas are tumors with dense capillary beds that can have connections to the coronary arteries. They are on the epicardial surface with intrusion into the myocardium.65 Hemangiomas can cause subpulmonary stenosis if they are located in the right ventricular outflow tract. Small hamartomas cause histiocytoid or oncocytic cardiomyopathy which is associated with severe and persistent ventricular arrhythmias. Usually, such tumors are subendocardial in location and comprised of pathognomonic nests of foamy appearing myocytes resembling macrophages.66 In infants with refractory arrhythmias, electrophysiological mapping and ablation may be required. Myocardial fibroma can be located in the myocardium or on the atrial wall or can involve the mitral valve and cause obstruction. Fibromas can also disrupt the conduction system and contribute to ventricular arrhythmias. Intrapericardial teratoma is a benign tumor attached to the base of the aorta. It is associated with mediastinal compression and pericardial effusion in the fetus, neonate, or young infant. Successful excision of intrapericardial teratoma has been reported, although large tumors can cause fetal death. Atrial myxomas have not been reported in the neonatal period. Surgical excision is required if there is obstruction to the inflow or outflow of the heart.

### Neonatal Marfan Syndrome

Neonatal Marfan syndrome (nMFS) is a rare condition and is genotypically and phenotypically quite distinct from the typical Marfan syndrome. The syndrome carries a poorer prognosis, as the cardiovascular complications associated with this disorder are associated with significant morbidity and mortality.77 Ninety percent of patients with nMFS die within the first year of life, signifying the poor prognosis. The diagnosis of nMFS, because of its clinical and phenotypic variability, is made following the criteria of skeletal, ocular, cardiovascular, cutaneous, neurologic, and pulmonary manifestations, as well as family history. Cardiac pathology is more severe in nMFS, with severe mitral and/ or tricuspid valve insufficiency leading to congestive cardiac failure from infancy. Aortic root dilatation and regurgitation are more common in classical Marfan syndrome.78 Other features such as joint contractures, megalocornea, iridodonesis, ectopia lentis, redundant loose skin, and crumpled ears are more common in the neonatal form compared to the classical form.

Most severe cases are caused by a sporadic mutation in a single germ cell of one parent. Mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15, encoding the protein fibrillin-1, cause Marfan syndrome. Mutations associated with nMFS have been consistently reported in exons 24 to 32 of the same chromosome. Mutations in the region of exons 25 and 26 are associated with a shorter survival in children diagnosed with nMFS before the age of 1 year.78 Genetic testing to
